content: Improvements in case-based surveillance systems are essential to accurately identify individuals who are lost to follow-up, those who experience adverse events, and those who develop immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Updated recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and monitoring are critical to addressing these challenges. Research priorities include understanding the impact of initiating ART in individuals with tuberculosis (TB) symptoms, excluding those with signs of meningitis, on mortality, TB and HIV outcomes, adverse events, IRIS, retention in care, and adherence. This research should also consider specific populations such as children, pregnant women, and breastfeeding women. Analyzing routine program data in countries implementing these approaches and conducting studies to optimize implementation, particularly among individuals with advanced HIV disease, would provide valuable insights. The Guideline Development Group has identified a key research gap: the role of prophylactic corticosteroids in reducing the incidence of IRIS among individuals with TB and HIV in public health settings, as well as determining the optimal timing for prophylaxis. While adjuvant corticosteroids are recommended for tuberculous meningitis, they are not recommended for individuals with HIV who have cryptococcal meningitis. Therefore, refining clinical approaches to corticosteroid use in HIV-associated meningitis is of critical importance. The Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes is collaborating with WHO Press to ensure maximum visibility of WHO products at major conferences, such as the International AIDS Society conferences and the Conferences for Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections. Following approval by the Guidelines Review Committee, updated guidelines will be made available on the WHO HIV website. These recommendations, along with other relevant guidance released since 2016, will be integrated into the updated consolidated HIV guidelines planned for release in July 2021. The publication will initially be available in English, with translations into other official languages developed in coordination with regional and country offices. The recommendations and supporting information will also be integrated into the WHO HIV Tx App, a free mobile application designed for easy access and reference. This app is globally available for download on major app stores. Additionally, printed materials, PDFs, and social media links will be used to disseminate key messages of WHO recommendations. Key annexes containing systematic reviews and other supporting information will be uploaded to the WHO website. Derivative products, such as slide sets, question-and-answer documents, and webinars with key stakeholders, will be developed to assist countries in adapting and implementing the guidelines in their specific contexts. The Department of Global HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes monitors the uptake of HIV-related recommendations through mechanisms such as the Global AIDS Monitoring framework, in-country surveys, and population-based HIV impact assessments. These provide indirect evidence of the impact of WHO recommendations. The Department will work with WHO regional and country offices to monitor the uptake and implementation of the guidelines. Potential barriers include delays in dissemination due to the time required for translation and limited resources in countries to change existing policies. The guidelines will be updated using a modular process. Ongoing scoping reviews are conducted to anticipate future guidance needs. When necessary, rapid guidance and technical and operational updates will complement the guideline updates. The standard GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) and PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome) processes were used for guideline development. Systematic reviews were conducted to address the PICO questions, complemented by supporting information from sources such as online values and preferences surveys commissioned by WHO, targeted literature reviews on feasibility, acceptability, costs, cost-effectiveness, and disease modeling. The GRADE method was used to rate the certainty of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. Certainty of evidence reflects the confidence that the reported estimates of effect match the actual effects of interest. The strength of a recommendation reflects the degree of confidence that the desirable effects (e.g., reduced morbidity and mortality, cost savings) outweigh the undesirable effects (e.g., potential harm, resource use). Additional considerations include resource use, cost implications, values and preferences of affected individuals, feasibility, acceptability, and the impact on equity and human rights. All systematic reviews followed PRISMA guidelines for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The outputs of the meta-analyses were displayed as relative estimates and absolute effect sizes per 1,000 people, along with the GRADE level of certainty of evidence (high, moderate, low, or very low) for each outcome.
